KEY MESSAGE 1...Some low stratus in the morning had kept a lid on 
temps early on, however, as we have gotten into the afternoon, ENC 
has become well mixed, allowing clouds to mix and scatter out 
bringing warmer temps to the region with highs getting into the 
upper 80s to low 90s. With dewpoints in the 70s AppTs will 
range around 100F this afternoon and again on Wednesday, though 
SWern zones have exceeded 105deg for a few hours today. As a
result Heat Advisory remains in effect for these areas this 
afternoon. Isolated to widely scattered showers and tstorms and 
increased cloud coverage from debris clouds will end the heat 
threat earlier in the day than previous days and have left the 
end time of the heat advisory at 6PM. Potential for additional 
cloud cover and storms Wed should keep T/MaxTs at bay, and 
therefore not anticipating heat advisory criteria to be reached 
at this moment on Wed.

KEY MESSAGE 2...With isolated to widely scattered showers and 
thunderstorms forecast this afternoon and evening, a brief reprieve 
from more widespread activity is forecast today. While we can't rule 
out a stronger gust today (40-60 mph) within the strongest storms as 
MLCAPE values get to around 2500-3500 J/kg this afternoon, think 
this threat would be far and few in between as a dry layer of air 
and lack of forcing likely keeps activity disorganized across 
the FA. SPC has an Enhanced risk (lvl 3/5) centered across the 
Mid-Atlantic, with a slight risk (lvl 2/5) stretching SW'ward 
into Wern TN. ENC is clipped with a sliver of Slight and 
Marginal risks (lvl 2 & 1/5). While PWATS are around 2" today 
given the isolated nature and lack of training storms with 
todays activity, also think the flash flooding threat is very 
low as well.

Biggest change today has been the slight delay compared to the
00Z suite of the frontal passage with the front not getting 
into the area until Thurs which has slightly delayed the 
heaviest precip until Thursday across ENC. 

As we get into Wed night/Thurs and into this weekend, 
previously mentioned frontal boundary will track across the 
area Thurs and stall offshore with multiple mid level shortwaves
tracking across the Mid-Atlantic into this weekend bringing 
elevated rain and thunderstorm chances to ENC over the next 
several days. Moisture increases ahead of this front with low to
midlevel flow opening up moisture advection channel from the E 
side of what is now Tropical Storm Bertha. The National 
Hurricane Center continues issuing advisories for Bertha, but 
poses no tropical threat to ENC at this time, as it is forecast 
to meander slowly W across the Nern Gulf of America. The 
greatest risk for strong to severe thunderstorms will be Wed 
associated with a prefrontal trough, with the threat shifting 
to more of a hydro threat Thurs. 

For Wed expect leftover cloudcover in the morning to mix out and
lift into the afternoon hours. With a warm and moist environment
in place across ENC through the day, this is forecast to allow 
for MLCAPE values to reach 2000-3000 J/kg in the afternoon 
hours. With a prefrontal trough likely setting up across ENC 
out ahead of the incoming front and the seabreeze moving inland 
this should be the focus for isolated to widely scattered 
showers and thunderstorms once again with activity near the 
coast in the morning and moving inland as the afternoon wears 
on. Once again there would be a low end threat for a wet 
microburst or strong downdraft wind gust (40-60 mph) within the
strongest storms. ENC is once again in a marginal risk for 
severe thunderstorms tomorrow with a sliver or NW'rn Martin 
County in a slight risk (levels 1 & 2 of 5). The severe risk 
decreases greatly on Thurs as ongoing rain and cloudcover likely
inhibits instability, but this threat then transitions to a 
flash flooding risk. 

Out ahead of the strong front, moisture is forecast to pool in 
ENC. This will allow the already high PWATS of around 2" to 
increase further closer to 2.25-2.75" on Wed and persist across 
the area through Thurs. As mentioned above, latest guidance has
slowed slightly with the frontal passage with this front likely
not entering into the area until Thurs morning. All available 
guidance has showers and thunderstorms developing and training 
along and just out ahead of the slow moving front Thurs. With 
PWAT's well over 2", a deep warm cloud layer, long skinny CAPEs,
and ample moisture forecast across ENC the environment will be 
primed for a flash flooding risk. This risk begins Wed and 
maximizes Thurs. WPC currently has the area under a slight risk
for flash flooding (level 2/4) for Wednesday with general 
rainfall amounts between 0.25-0.75" possible with the highest 
amounts focused along the northern tier of counties.

However, as we get into Thurs most available deterministic and
AI guidance is suggesting 24 hour rainfall totals between 2-4"
